newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance jitters recede, but long haul ahead.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance jitters recede, but long haul ahead.

text.p: One of the keynote speeches at a gathering of Thai finance executives this weekend was all about stress control and how to deal with anxiety.
"Don't get worked up, worrying that the central bank will issue a new list of troubled companies and that yours might be one of them," quipped psychiatrist Udomsil Srisangnam.

After a frantic week of massive deposit withdrawals from cash-strapped finance companies, a plunge in stock market values and a general wobble of confidence in Thailand's much-admired economic miracle, Udomsil's soothing advice was timely.

Around the corner from the conference hall in a swanky hotel at this seaside resort, a palmist sat ready to read fortunes -- or perhaps even misfortunes. But none of the money men were relying on such quaint devices to see their way ahead.

Instead, they were brimming with confidence that an industry overhaul, unveiled by Thai authorities in the midst of market turmoil, would restore confidence in both the country's weakened financial institutions and its economy.
"Last week friends kept ringing me, asking if everything was okay," said TSFC Securities President Akarat Na Ranong. "I think the measures will be enough to rebuild public confidence."
Foreign analysts were not so sure that the crisis was over.

"It could well drag on for a few more months. We might see some Thai macroeconomic indicators improve, but this is a different microeconomic problem that will linger on until investors are totally convinced," said the head of research at a foreign brokerage.
Last Monday the authorities ordered 10 finance companies, hard-hit by a liquidity crunch, to raise capital by a total of 8.25 billion baht ($317 million).
They also toughened loan-loss reserve requirements for the country's 15 banks and 91 finance firms, many of which have huge exposure to the bloated and crisis-torn real estate market.

The institutions' woes have been exacerbated by an economic slowdown after a decade of almost double-digit annual growth and the central bank's high interest rate policy to deter attacks on the baht, which was hit by devaluation rumours last month. The government followed up its dose of bitter pills with an announcement that it would issue zero-coupon bonds to take troubled property loans off finance companies' balance sheet.
For good measure, central bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond moved to reassure wavering foreign investors that currency stability remained a top policy priority.

He also said the country's current account deficit, which has partly contributed to speculation against the baht, would narrow to less than 7.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year from 8.0 percent in 1996.

Thailand's stock market index, which has lost half its value in the past year, tumbled last week amid fears about the finance sector's health. But shares moved higher on Friday as confidence trickled back, cutting its loss for the week to 4.96 percent.
Analysts said they expected a much less volatile market next week, with buying interest from bargain hunters.
Still, no one was popping champagne at the Pattaya meeting.

"We got through a battle, sure, but there is still a long war to fight," said one executive at the meeting, reeling off a list of systemic flaws in an industry which had grown complacent about easy profit during years of economic boom.

Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond told the conference that the crisis was "a blessing in disguise" because it would bring reckless lending to heel and force a rationalisation of the industry through a spate of mergers.
